judged_by: Carried over from qwen3-4b-harness-slots/coverage (Matched by a Claude Opus 5.5 agent on 2026-11-22; not yet checked by the labeler.) Claims the harness dropped are removed; repaired quotes were not judged for support.

question.note: Phrased as 'the paper argues that' climate moderates, but the substance and quote are the study's goal; the paper's title frames it as climate's moderating role.

flags.text: Says 'liberal political climates reduce vaccine hesitancy among politically conservative individuals'. The paper reports an association and states it 'cannot assume causal or directional associations' (p.10).

question.note: A finding (conservative half of C1) restated in the question slot in causal form; no credit.

flags.text: Says booster likelihood 'is influenced by' conservatism and regional climate. The paper reports associations and an interaction (OR = .84) and allows only a hedged 'may impact' for environmental factors.

question.note: A vague restatement of a booster finding in the question slot; does not state the shape of F3, so no misplaced credit.
Restates only the liberal half of F3 (liberals boosted regardless of climate) in the question slot; too partial for misplaced credit.

Restates part of F4 (interaction not significant for initial vaccination, unlike booster status) in the question slot, without the mandates explanation; too partial for misplaced credit. Accurate to the paper.

central_claim.note: Conservative half of C1 (hesitancy); liberals' low hesitancy regardless of climate is not stated here. 'Moderates the effect' not flagged: the paper speaks of moderation and of 'average effects'.
Booster half of C1, both liberal and conservative parts. 'Significantly higher' for liberals is loose (the paper says 'more likely'), not flagged.
Booster percentages (over 65% liberals regardless; 60% vs under 35% for the most conservative) match p.8.

evidence.note: Booster hesitancy items from a 2022 survey (ref. 25): accurate, not in the gold (E5 covers the vaccine hesitancy scale).
CFA and alpha = .93 for both scales: accurate to p.5, not in the gold.
Linear and logistic regressions with controls, but no mention of the conservatism by climate interaction term. Lists controls without gender; minor.
Self-reported vaccine and booster status (half of E5); the hesitancy scale is not named. Quote is a fragment about the booster item.
Zip-code exclusions and final N = 683, without the Qualtrics screening numbers.
Convenience sample through Qualtrics Panels; E1 also credited in entry [0].

key_findings.note: Conservative half of the hesitancy interaction; liberals-regardless part missing.

Liberal half of F3. The quote given (p.10, booster hesitancy slightly lower for liberals in conservative climates) does not support the claim about booster receipt; the p.8 passage would. 'Significantly higher' is loose wording.
Conservative half of F3, with the 60% vs under 35% quote.
Says the interaction is significant for booster hesitancy and booster status (p.10), without the shape; F3 already partly credited in [1] and [2].

theoretical_positioning.note: Names only the climate literature (broadened to 'health behaviors'; the paper says COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake) and the extension by testing moderation.
Prior research treated orientation or climate separately; the paper adds their interaction. 'Refinement' is close enough to the paper's 'novel' extension.

flags.text: Says the paper disputes a claim that political climate has no effect on vaccine hesitancy. The paper cites no such claim; it builds on prior studies that found climate associated with hesitancy and uptake (refs 19-21).

interlocutor_claim.note: Builds on the conservatism-hesitancy association. The quote is the paper's own result from the abstract rather than the cited literature.

flags.text: Says the paper challenges the idea that political orientation alone determines vaccine behavior. No cited work claims this; the paper builds on studies of orientation and of climate separately (p.2, p.10).
Says regional climate 'significantly influences conservative individuals' decisions to receive boosters'. The paper reports an association and rules out causal or directional readings (p.10).
